In their first friendly since reaching the 2014 World Cup, Scotland take on Italy in Genoa hoping to carry momentum into their play-off second leg against Croatia next month. After beating France and Wales away recently as part pf qualifying for the major tournament finals, Gordon Strachan's men were beaten against Costa Rica before hammering Panama either side of an underwhelming Nations League campaign where they won one and lost both group games after drawing their opener with Albania. However, their win over Israel in March set up a two legged tie with Croatia which will determine who lines up at Russia 2018. They are unbeaten in 16 matches now and hope a victory of any sort would help them prepare for life without Celtic striker Leigh Griffiths - the country's top scorer over the past three years. Defeat against the Azzurri tonight could dent that positivity as well as potentially put pressure on the manager heading into next month's big two legged ties when the winner goes through to face Cristiano Ronaldo's Portugal or Albania for a shot at playing Iceland in June. For the hosts, coach Roberto Mancini can have little complaints regarding his forward options but he certainly could do without some of this season's early defensive gaffes. Despite having played five friendlies since he took charge last month, they cannot be said to be in great form whatsoever having drawn all four home fixtures and winning just one on the road after conceding late and ending each contest scoreless. It must get better soon for the Italian national team but perhaps tonight's match will demonstrate exactly why Strachan wants time off rather than immediate football management jobs! Sir Thomas Joseph Madden PC QC (1905 – 7 February 2003) was a Northern Irish politician and statesman who was most prominent during the period from 1968 to 1973 as Secretary of State for Northern Ireland, where he presided over the period that saw the most serious sectarian unrest in Northern Ireland since independence in 1916 which led directly up to the establishment of Direct Rule by Westminster governments and the subsequent collapse of Stormont under Unionist Prime Minister Faulkner's regime. During this time, he negotiated with the Nationalist leadership on reforming local government there.^{[1]} Madden later served as Chairman^{[2]}^{[3]}^{[4]}^{[5]}^{[6]}^{[7]}^{[8]} of the Constitutional Convention, set up by Prime Minister Harold Wilson immediately after his election defeat in 1970, as one alternative method devolved power back to Stormont should it succeed (it failed), before finally settling on what became the Sunningdale Agreement a year earlier also known as "The Sunningdale Executive." Sir Tom did not approve of the agreement; both because it brought about de facto joint rule between Britain & Eire without referendum to the affected population & also due to some perceived similarities with former attempts at Home Rule such as the Anglo-Irish Treaty of 1921. His disapproval extended even so far as calling Margaret Thatcher - herself originally a member of Heaths Cabinet while all these events occurred yet resigned when their direction changed with her own expulsion from cabinet two years previously following Labour Party split owing largely to conflicting views upon Europe - 'a fool' publicly stating 'her comments towards me were too ignorant for words'.

Axone is a 2019 Indian comedy-drama film directed by Nicholas Kharkongor and produced by Yoodlee Films, Saregama India's film division. The film stars Sayani Gupta, Vinay Pathak, Lin Laishram, Dolly Ahluwalia, Adil Hussain, Lanuakum Ao, Tenzin Dalha, and Rohan Joshi. The film follows Northeast Indian migrants in New Delhi, in their attempt to organize a wedding party. The film premiered at the London Film Festival on 2 October 2019. Plot
The story tells of a group of migrants from Northeast India to Delhi, Upasana (Sayani Gupta), Chanbi (Lin Laishram), and Zorem, who are trying to help their friend Minam (Asenla Jamir) with her wedding preparations. Minam, who shares a flat with Upasana, Chanbi, and others from their region, is called away suddenly for an interview. Meanwhile, her friends try to find an ingredient to make 'Axone,' a special dish that they want for the wedding. The friends face various difficulties as they attempt to plan the wedding and prepare Axone. The other tenants object and the landlord's mother-in-law enforces her rule against parties or spicy cooking in the flat. They decide to hold the wedding at Chanbi's boyfriend Bendang's flat, but finding a way to cook Axone without drawing the attention of locals brings comical problems.

As the story opens, Lia, 15, is at her great-grandmother Sarah's bedside. Delirious, the old woman begins to speak of Graymoss Plantation, the Louisiana family estate left unoccupied for decades because of a "terrible, fearful evil." After the woman's death, Lia discovers that the house has been willed to her mother, who plans to move the family in and adopt a group of hard-to-place children. Lia is against this idea and vows to prove to her mother that the house is truly haunted. She learns that the ghostly occurrences are well documented and that several locals oppose the family taking up residence at Graymoss. Could one of these people be staging the hauntings? Lia has a change of heart, however, after she meets the children her parents want to care for and resolves to take on the ghosts herself. Aided by a collection of Edgar Allan Poe's stories, she eventually succeeds in driving the spirits away. The ghosts are reminiscent of those in Shirley Jackson's classic The Haunting of Hill House, whispering through the walls and sending books flying through the air. The novel ends somewhat abruptly, and a potentially interesting romantic relationship fizzles out completely, but this is still a page-turner that will satisfy mystery and ghost story fans.

Twenty-three years old Claud Bannister has just failed his exam to be an accountant and is determined to give up his studies and become a writer. He is introduced to Laura Thornby at a concert. Laura is forty-five, single and a notorious meddler. When she hears about Claud's plans, and learns that he is living with his mother, Laura immediately starts rearranging his life. In no time Claud finds himself installed in a rented loft and making a living by selling antiques from a stall in the market. Laura becomes so interested in Claud's welfare, and her own, that she even ends up in bed with him. When Laura isn't visiting Claud in his loft, and he isn't working in the market, he is busy working on his novel, just as Laura had planned. But even Laura Thornby cannot foresee everything. Her affairs have always been brief and she has always been in total control, but with Claud she begins to lose control. When she sees what Claud has written, she realizes that he has a talent, and that she herself merely is playing second fiddle to his fictional characters.

A friend sets Theresa up on a blind date with a nice guy named Tony who works in the computer industry. It is awkward, but not too awkward as Theresa accepts a second date. (They even find a couple things in common such as both being from the Midwest.) By the end of this date, she realizes that he is not right for her and politely excuses herself from the date. Tony continues to intrude further into Theresa’s life, with unexpected visits to Theresa’s office and unsettling phone messages at her home. Theresa starts to worry as she realizes that Tony knows where she lives. At her co-worker's urging, she calls the police, but when Officer Beck investigates, Theresa realizes there is not much that the police can do. Beck suggests moving out of her apartment and changing her name. Despite all her efforts to avoid him by hiding in her work and opening up to her colleagues, she eventually realizes that he has and will always have control over her life. She eventually loses everything, including her identity, humanity, and will, as she changes her name and moves out of New York City to Denver, a shadow of the woman she once was.

Russian energy giant Gazprom is suing the Isle of Man government for more than $36m for alleged unpaid taxes for 2005. It is seeking the money for work in the Russian Arctic in 2005 carried out by a company registered in the British Crown dependency.
The Russian oil and gas giant is one of the largest companies in the world and has a share price of over $100bn. Gazprom is claiming the Isle of Man breached a 2003 treaty between the two countries, which regulates the tax position of Gazprom and its subsidiaries.
The Russian firm claims the Isle of Man breached the treaty in the assessment of its 2005 income tax liability and seeks a refund of the $36.2m in tax paid.
An Isle of Man tax spokeswoman said it will "robustly defend" Gazprom's claims and would only comment after all legal hearings had been concluded.

In 2028 America has been reduced to rubble by a computer virus dubbed "The Mother." A cyber-terrorist named Thomas Gabriel, who calls himself 'Tripwire', steals a flash drive that he plans to use to put his plan into action. John McClane, who left active duty ten years ago, lives in an empty police station in Columbus, Ohio. His only friends are a hacker named Farrell (Mamet) and a fellow cop that was on vacation when the other officers were killed in an early incident. John gets a call from his wife (who now owns her own company) in New York City, and she tells him that someone has kidnapped her assistant. He takes off to New York, where he runs into his wife at the local police station. Later, John and his wife have to fight, in John's words, "an insane and powerful group of electronic terrorists" to save the United States as it has been plunged back into a techno-feudal dark age.

Gravy oamc is made up mostly of browned ground beef that's been cooked down in some type of broth (lentils are best, but whatever you have – feel free to make it vegetarian). Then you top this with your choice of vegetables and maybe onions or mushrooms! You can even use gluten-free bread crumbs if you're not into a whole grain flour version of hearty meatloaf. And I've also made my own beef bouillon so its much healthier – just mix the bouillon cubes and oil together until everything is well combined. All of these factors work really well when cooked at high heat in an oven and allow us to get the benefits of the healthy fats we're eating without adding in added sugar. Enjoy it as a main course or snack on top of brown rice! It's such a great way to use up leftover roast chicken or lentil stew, too. Be sure to follow alltherestaurants.com on Instagram for daily recipe updates throughout the week to find all the other ways this cheesy, meatloaf worthy meal makes me happy :) Also be advised a portion includes about 1/2 cup mashed potatoes to replace potato chips - because yes… I do eat potatoes. 🙂

Slumdog Millionaire is an engaging story, and despite its brutalities, it is encouraging because of the possibility of redemption and happiness. It is also a highly creative film, using the devices of a game show to weave together the stories of Jamal's life, and to raise the tension level as he progresses from one stage to the next. The device also allows for the introduction, one by one, of the key characters in Jamal's life, and their stories are skilfully interwoven in the game show. The direction is superb, as is the acting, and the music is uplifting. This is a ground-level view of India, warts and all, but it ends up with a message of hope, and that is a message we can all endorse.

Novak Djokovic is out of Wimbledon for the first time since 2010, leaving Andy Roddick to face Jo-Wilfried Tsonga in the third round on Monday.
Djokovic suffered a straight sets loss to Swiss champion Roger Federer in the quarterfinals at the Australian Open earlier this year. With Federer also advanced to the semifinals of Wimbledon, it will be a battle between two record holders this summer.
Federer holds the most Grand Slam titles with 20, while Djokovic has won four and reached the finals in five. The other Grand Slam champs remaining are Stanislas Wawrinka and Rafael Nadal, who was forced to withdraw from the tournament before its start due to an injury.
As they chase their first major title of the season, Roddick and Tsonga have never faced each other on grass. Roddick lost to James Blake last year in the fourth round, while Tsonga made a second-round exit in 2009.
This marks their fifth meeting overall, with each player winning twice previously. However, all those matches took place indoors on hard courts.
"I don't think that makes any difference," Roddick said. "We both played pretty well on grass over the past few years."

Slouching Towards Gomorrah: Modern Liberalism and American Decline is a 1996 non-fiction book by Robert H. Bork, a former United States Court of Appeals judge. Bork's thesis in the book is that U.S. and more generally Western culture is in a state of decline and that the cause of this decline is modern liberalism and the rise of the New Left. Specifically, he attacks modern liberalism for what he describes as its dual emphases on radical egalitarianism and radical individualism. The title of the book is a play on the last couplet of W. B. Yeats's poem "The Second Coming": "And what rough beast, its hour come round at last, / Slouches towards Bethlehem to be born?" Bork contends that the "rough beast of decadence … now sends us slouching towards our new home, not Bethlehem but Gomorrah." More directly, the title borrows from Joan Didion's Slouching Towards Bethlehem. Overview
Bork first traces the rapid expansion of modern liberalism that occurred during the 1960s, arguing that this legacy of radicalism demonstrates that the precepts of modern liberalism are antithetical to the rest of the U.S. political tradition. He then attacks a variety of social, cultural, and political experiences as evidence of U.S. cultural decline and degeneracy. Among these are affirmative action, increased violence in and sexualization of mass media, the legalization of abortion, pressure to legalize assisted suicide and euthanasia, feminism and the decline of religion. Bork, himself a rejected nominee of President Ronald Reagan to the United States Supreme Court, also criticizes that institution and argues that the judiciary and liberal judicial activism are catalysts for U.S. cultural corruption.

Vibration cooking, sometimes called ultrasound cavitation cooking is a method of cooking food via high frequency ultrasound waves. It has been researched for several years in the U.S., the Netherlands and other countries, but remains rare in American and European kitchens. The use of sound waves, such as those generated by ultrasound, to cook food may be more useful for industrial applications than domestic applications.
The method was developed by Professor Nicholas Chriss, Associate Professor Daniel Grossman and their co-workers at the University of Houston in 1996. It's used for cooking by applying high power sound waves to the food, which creates microscopic bubbles that oscillate and then burst. The process occurs at a temperature of about 45 °C (113 °F), much lower than conventional cooking methods, which makes it appealing to some, as it preserves natural protein, flavor, and nutrients and allows more delicate foods like fruits, vegetables, and eggs to be cooked.

In this method of cooking, microwaves and radiowaves are bombarded on food. The waves penetrate right into the cells of the food, which become energized when the waves interact with the moisture in the food. As an effect, water-based foods become soft. This mechanism provides advantages over traditional cooking methods. There is no possibility of overcooking. In ultrasonic cooking, there is no heat build-up and there is a uniform cooking of food throughout. Moreover, the foods cooked this way provide more moisture and have a fresh texture. The cooking process is fast as the sound waves travel through the water content in foods in comparison to electric waves. Hence, food in water-based solution can cook much faster than those in fat based solution.

K-Net: Towards Unified Image Segmentation.

Image classification based on deep convolutional neural networks (with non-linear feature transformation) is commonly employed for tasks such as face and object recognition. However, these models suffer from severe tradeoffs in the quality of the predictions and the quality of the training data. We present a new model with high performance while having an expressive and simple structure which makes it highly suitable for a variety of tasks. We apply K-Net to a large dataset of photos to identify the scene from their faces. We find that the model significantly outperforms other state of the art approaches by more than two orders of magnitude and outperforms other models with larger training datasets by between 8 and 25 times.


We demonstrate the robustness of the neural network by testing its performance (on a set of 10K images) on a set of 10K images (10 sets of 20 images each) taken from the same dataset and a set of 10000 images from a second dataset which was taken from the same set of pictures with the same camera by a different photographer. Although the model is described on small data sets, we found that on large training datasets this model outperforms both the state of the art and popular algorithms on both datasets. We demonstrate that the K-Net model is general and scalable.

As an adult who regularly interacts with teenagers, both online and offline, I've noticed an increasing trend of disrespectful and rude behaviors emanating from some of them. This is not to say all teenagers are this way, but the growing penchant for unkindness, condescension, lack of basic etiquette, and even outright verbal abuse rightfully incites concern.

Of course, teenagers are in a phase where they are forming their identities and navigating societal rules, and it's normal for some rebellious or challenging attitudes to surface. However, the level of intensity seems to have escalated recently, surpassing what we might mark as 'typical' teenage rebellion or low inhibitions due to developing emotional intelligence.

I've observed this in various settings: from schools to public places and extensively on social media platforms. Some engage in mockery, ridicule, or foul language against peers, adults, or even authority figures. Others exhibit an almost nonchalant disregard for other people's feelings or work. 

I have a few theories which could attribute to this conduct, such as a lack of sufficient role models, the influence of aggressive or disrespectful behavior viewed in media, not getting held accountable for their actions, or the prevailing sense of anonymity on the internet that emboldens them.

For the record, I am aware that not all teenagers are rude. Many are respectful and a real joy to interact with. However, I'm focusing here on those who show uncalled-for rudeness. It's worrying and something that I believe needs to be addressed more effectively.

I'm curious to hear your thoughts. Have you noticed this trend as well? Is it symptomatic of larger societal issues or perhaps the result of changing trends in parenting?

French actress Audrey Tautou has been cast as Mona Lisa in an upcoming movie about Leonardo da Vinci, according to reports.

The 31-year-old will play the subject of one of the world's most famous paintings in the biopic by director James Cameron.

He added that she would be perfect for the role because she looked like the painting.

"Her face is very similar to the portrait," he said.

Tautou - who won international acclaim with her performance in Jean-Pierre Jeunet's Amelie - is currently shooting a comedy called Coco Before Chanel.

Difference-in-differences (DID) is a method to evaluate the effect of a
treatment. In its basic version, a "control group" is untreated at two dates,
whereas a "treatment group" becomes fully treated at the second date. However,
in many applications of the DID method, the treatment rate only increases more
in the treatment group. In such fuzzy designs, a popular estimator of treatment
effects is the DID of the outcome divided by the DID of the treatment. We show
that this ratio identifies a local average treatment effect only if two
homogeneous treatment effect assumptions are satisfied. We then propose two
alternative estimands that do not rely on any assumption on treatment effects,
and that can be used when the treatment rate does not change over time in the
control group. We prove that the corresponding estimators are asymptotically
normal. Finally, we use our results to revisit Duflo (2001).

In microscopic mechanical systems interactions between elastic structures are
often mediated by the hydrodynamics of a solvent fluid. At microscopic scales
the elastic structures are also subject to thermal fluctuations. Stochastic
numerical methods are developed based on multigrid which allow for the
efficient computation of both the hydrodynamic interactions in the presence of
walls and the thermal fluctuations. The presented stochastic multigrid approach
provides efficient real-space numerical methods for generating the required
stochastic driving fields with long-range correlations consistent with
statistical mechanics. The presented approach also allows for the use of
spatially adaptive meshes in resolving the hydrodynamic interactions. Numerical
results are presented which show the methods perform in practice with a
computational complexity of O(N log(N)).

Vibration Cooking: Or, the Travel Notes of a Geechee Girl is the 1970 debut book by Vertamae Smart-Grosvenor and combines recipes with storytelling. It was published by Doubleday. A second edition was published in 1986, and a third edition was published in 1992. The University of Georgia published another edition in 2011. Smart-Grosvenor went on to publish more cookbooks after Vibration Cooking. Vibration Cooking raised awareness about Gullah culture. Scholar Anne E. Goldman compared Vibration Cooking with Jessica Harris' Iron Pots and Wooden Spoons, arguing that, in both books, "the model of the self... is historicized by being developed in the context of colonialism." Scholar Lewis V. Baldwin recommended Vibration Cooking for its "interesting and brilliant insights on the social significance of food and eating and their relationship to 'place' in a southern context." The book inspired filmmaker Julie Dash to make the film Daughters of the Dust, which won awards at the Sundance Film Festival. See also

Steve Bechtel (born March 19, 1970) is a rock climber, coach, and author based in Lander, Wyoming. He has been important in developing climbing around the region since the 1990s. Bechtel is considered a prime suspect in the unsolved disappearance of his first wife, Amy Wroe Bechtel. Biography
Bechtel was born in Casper, Wyoming. As a teenager, Bechtel began to rock climb in central Wyoming, inspired by the sport climbing then popular in Europe. He later referred to these experiences as "great [opportunities] as a young person to see people at the cutting edge of the sport." His interest in Lander, Wyoming was piqued in the summer of 1990 when he heard about the limestone in the Black Hills, which was considered favorable for rock climbing. After two brief visits there that same year, Bechtel decided to move there the following year. Aside from a short period in the early 2000s when he lived in Salt Lake City, Utah, Bechtel has since resided permanently in Lander. He cited the Sinks Main Wall as the reason he settled permanently in the town.
